In [[mathematics]], the '''free category''' or '''path category''' generated by a [[directed graph]] or [[quiver (mathematics)|quiver]] is the [[category (category theory)|category]] that results from freely concatenating arrows together, whenever the target of one arrow is the source of the next.

More precisely, the objects of the category are the vertices of the quiver, and the morphisms are paths between objects. Here, a '''path''' is defined as a [[finite sequence]]
:<math>V_0\xrightarrow{\;\;E_0\;\;} V_1\xrightarrow{\;\;E_1\;\;} 
 \cdots \xrightarrow{E_{n-1}} V_n </math>
where <math>V_k</math> is a vertex of the quiver, <math>E_k</math> is an edge of the quiver, and ''n'' ranges over the non-negative integers. For every vertex <math>V</math> of the quiver, there is an "empty path" which constitutes the identity morphisms of the category.

The composition operation is concatenation of paths. Given paths
:<math>V_0\xrightarrow{E_0}\cdots\xrightarrow{E_{n-1}} V_n,\quad V_n\xrightarrow{F_0}W_0\xrightarrow{F_1}\cdots\xrightarrow{F_{m}} W_m,</math>
their composition is
:<math>\left(V_n\xrightarrow{F_0}W_0\xrightarrow{F_1}\cdots\xrightarrow{F_{m}} W_m \right) \circ \left(V_0\xrightarrow{E_0}\cdots\xrightarrow{E_{n-1}} V_n \right) := V_0\xrightarrow{E_0}\cdots\xrightarrow{E_{n-1}} V_n\xrightarrow{F_0}W_0\xrightarrow{F_1}\cdots\xrightarrow{F_{m}} W_m</math>.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|title=Category theory|last=Awodey|first=Steve|date=2010|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0199237180|edition=2nd|location=Oxford|pages=20–24|oclc=740446073}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite book|title=[[Categories for the Working Mathematician]]|last=Mac Lane|first=Saunders|author-link=Saunders Mac Lane|date=1978|publisher=Springer New York|isbn=1441931236|edition=Second|location=New York, NY|pages=49–51|oclc=851741862}}</ref>

Note that the result of the composition starts with the right operand of the composition, and ends with its left operand.

== Examples ==
* If {{var|Q}} is the quiver with one vertex and one edge {{var|f}} from that object to itself, then the free category on {{var|Q}} has as arrows {{var|1}}, {{var|f}}, {{var|f}}∘{{var|f}},{{var|f}}∘{{var|f}}∘{{var|f}}, etc.<ref name=":1"/>
* Let {{var|Q}} be the quiver with two vertices {{var|a}}, {{var|b}} and two edges {{var|e}}, {{var|f}} from {{var|a}} to {{var|b}} and {{var|b}} to {{var|a}}, respectively. Then the free category on {{var|Q}} has two identity arrows and an arrow for every finite sequence of alternating {{var|e}}s and {{var|f}}s, including: {{var|e}}, {{var|f}}, {{var|e}}∘{{var|f}}, {{var|f}}∘{{var|e}}, {{var|f}}∘{{var|e}}∘{{var|f}}, {{var|e}}∘{{var|f}}∘{{var|e}}, etc.<ref name=":0" />
* If {{var|Q}} is the quiver <math>a\xrightarrow{f}b\xrightarrow{g}c</math>, then the free category on {{var|Q}} has (in addition to three identity arrows), arrows {{var|f}}, {{var|g}}, and {{var|g}}∘{{var|f}}.
* If a quiver {{var|Q}} has only one vertex, then the free category on {{var|Q}} has only one object, and corresponds to the [[free monoid]] on the edges of {{var|Q}}.<ref name=":0" />

==Properties==
The [[category of small categories]] '''Cat''' has a [[forgetful functor]] {{var|U}} into the quiver category '''Quiv''':

:{{var|U}} : '''Cat''' → '''Quiv'''

which takes objects to vertices and morphisms to arrows. Intuitively, {{var|U}} "[forgets] which arrows are composites and which are identities".<ref name=":1" /> This forgetful functor is [[right adjoint]] to the functor sending a quiver to the corresponding free category.

===Universal property===

The free category on a quiver can be described [[up to]] [[Equivalence of categories|isomorphism]] by a [[universal property]]. Let {{var|C}} : '''Quiv''' → '''Cat''' be the functor that takes a quiver to the free category on that quiver (as described above), let {{var|U}} be the forgetful functor defined above, and let {{var|G}} be any quiver. Then there is a [[graph homomorphism]] {{var|I}} : {{var|G}} → {{var|U}}({{var|C}}({{var|G}})) and given any category '''D''' and any graph homomorphism {{var|F}} : {{var|G}} → {{var|U(D)}}, there is a unique functor {{var|F'}} : {{var|C}}({{var|G}}) → '''D''' such that {{var|U}}({{var|F'}})∘{{var|I}}={{var|F}}, i.e. the following diagram [[Commutative diagram|commutes]]:

[[Image:Free-category-ump.svg|300px|class=skin-invert]]

The functor {{var|C}} is [[left adjoint]] to the forgetful functor {{var|U}}.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /><ref>{{nlab|id=free+category|title=free category}}</ref>
